steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a 3D point-cloud object detection paper. It should explain the main problems with outdoor LiDAR detection datasets and how existing data augmentation handles them, then present our gradient-based voxel selection method (GraVoS), what it does to the data, the networks we tested it on, and a list of contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- 3D object detection and LiDAR point clouds
- Three challenges in outdoor point cloud detection datasets
- How existing augmentation handles each challenge (and its limits)
- Our idea: network-dependent selection of meaningful voxels (GraVoS)
- Effect of the selection and results on four networks
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- 3D object detection and LiDAR point clouds
  - growing importance in industry + academia; applications: autonomous driving, robotics
  - LiDAR = de-facto standard sensor for outdoor 3D scenes (figure)
  - output: sparse, irregular point clouds; used in many perception/understanding tasks
- Three challenges in outdoor point cloud detection datasets
  - (1) small datasets, in number of scenes
  - (2) many points in scene vs few points on objects; hundreds of thousands / millions of points, only a handful of objects
  - (3) class imbalance -> lower accuracy on infrequent classes
- Existing augmentation per challenge
  - (1) global ops on whole cloud: rotation along Z-axis, random flips along X-axis, coordinate scaling; methods for (2),(3) indirectly solve (1) too
  - (2) local ops on object points: random point drop out, frustum drop out, additive noise, intra-object mixing, swapping regions between objects
  - (3) (+ (2)) paste ground-truth objects from other point clouds -> mitigates imbalance
  - but ignores the network architecture; Reuse et al.: local and global augmentation depends on dataset AND network architecture -> network-dependent augmentation is beneficial
- Our idea
  - novel network-dependent data modification, addresses challenges 2 and 3 (1 indirectly, like prior work)
  - learn subset of scene elements meaningful for detection; meaningful defined w.r.t. the network, not only the scene (in line with Reuse et al.)
  - input only the subset -> fewer elements, better class balance per scene
  - focus on SoTA networks that voxelize point clouds first; voxels reduce input size (only occupied voxels processed) -> very large scenes; also impose structure
  - meaningful voxels = where model "struggles" to locate objects -> gradients decide -> Gradient-based Voxel Selection (GraVoS)
- Effect of selection
  - discarded voxels mostly background; few from prevalent classes, almost none from non-prevalent
  - contrast with dropout augmentation (random removal)
  - figure: point cloud (cyan), selected subset (salmon; points = voxel centers): far fewer background points, more on Car (most prevalent), almost all on Pedestrian and Cyclist
- Results
  - general, any voxel-based network; no additional inference time cost
  - four SoTA networks: SECOND, Part-A^{2}, Voxel R-CNN, CenterPoint; KITTI dataset
  - all improve, esp. difficult Pedestrian and Cyclist
  - e.g. Part-A^{2}, moderate subset: +2.32% Cyclist, +1.15% Pedestrian = error reduction 8.20% & 2.77%
- Contributions
  - novel generic "meaningful" voxel selection (Gradient-based Voxel Selection)
  - training procedure using selected voxels, no additional data; combines info from different training stages
  - improved performance of four voxel-based SoTA methods; copes with class imbalance and foreground-background imbalance

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
3D object detection is getting more and more important in industry and in academia, because it has a lot of applications, for example autonomous driving and robotics. For capturing 3D outdoor scenes, LiDAR sensors are the de-facto standard devices (see Fig.). LiDAR sensors produce 3D point clouds that are sparse and irregular, and these point clouds are used in many scene perception and scene understanding tasks.

Outdoor point cloud datasets for detection have three main challenges. The first one is that the datasets are small, in terms of the number of scenes. The second one is that there is a large number of points in the scene but only a small number of points on the training examples, which are the objects. One scene can have hundreds of thousands of points, or even millions, but only a handful of objects. The third challenge is class imbalance, which means some classes can have a lot more instances than other classes. This often leads to lower predictive accuracy for the classes that are infrequent.

For the first challenge, it was proposed to enrich the dataset during training with global operations that are applied to the whole point cloud, like rotation along the Z-axis, random flips along the X-axis and coordinate scaling. Most methods that solve the second and third challenges also solve the first challenge indirectly.

For the second challenge, the suggestion is to augment the scene with local operations, which are applied to the points of individual objects. Local operations are things like random point drop out, frustum drop out, additive noise added to the object, intra-object mixing, and swapping regions between different objects.

For the third challenge, and also the second one, other works propose to add ground-truth objects from other point clouds to the scene for training. This kind of augmentation does mitigate the imbalance. But it does not take the network architecture into account. Reuse et al. show with a series of experiments that both local and global data augmentation for 3D object detection depend strongly on the dataset and also on the network architecture. So augmentations that depend on the network are beneficial.

We present a new data modification approach that is network-dependent and addresses the second and third challenges. (The first challenge we address indirectly, like prior work.) The main idea is to learn a subset of the elements of the scene which are meaningful for object detection. In line with the observation of Reuse et al., we define meaningfulness in the context of the network and not only of the scene. If we only consider this subset as the input, we can decrease the number of elements in the scene and we can also increase the class balance inside a given scene.

- voxel-based SoTA networks: voxelize first; reduces input size (only occupied voxels processed) -> extremely large scenes; also imposes structure
- meaningful voxels = where model "struggles" to locate objects -> gradients -> Gradient-based Voxel Selection (GraVoS)
- removing non-informative voxels: mostly background discarded; few prevalent-class voxels, almost no non-prevalent; vs dropout (random)
- figure: point cloud (cyan), selected subset (salmon, points = voxel centers): fewer background, more Car, almost all Pedestrian/Cyclist
- general for voxel-based nets, no extra inference cost; SECOND, Part-A^{2}, Voxel R-CNN, CenterPoint on KITTI; all improve esp. Pedestrian, Cyclist; Part-A^{2} moderate: +2.32% / +1.15% (Cyclist / Pedestrian), error reduction 8.20% / 2.77%
- contributions: generic meaningful voxel selection; training procedure w/o additional data, combining training stages; improved four voxel-based SoTA methods, coping with class and foreground-background imbalance

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
3D object detection is getting more and more important in industry and in academia, because it has a lot of applications, for example autonomous driving and robotics. For capturing 3D outdoor scenes, LiDAR sensors are the de-facto standard devices (see Fig.). LiDAR sensors produce 3D point clouds that are sparse and irregular, and these point clouds are used in many scene perception and scene understanding tasks.

Outdoor point cloud datasets for detection have three main challenges. The first one is that the datasets are small, in terms of the number of scenes. The second one is that there is a large number of points in the scene but only a small number of points on the training examples, which are the objects. One scene can have hundreds of thousands of points, or even millions, but only a handful of objects. The third challenge is class imbalance, which means some classes can have a lot more instances than other classes. This often leads to lower predictive accuracy for the classes that are infrequent.

For the first challenge, it was proposed to enrich the dataset during training with global operations that are applied to the whole point cloud, like rotation along the Z-axis, random flips along the X-axis and coordinate scaling. Most methods that solve the second and third challenges also solve the first challenge indirectly.

For the second challenge, the suggestion is to augment the scene with local operations, which are applied to the points of individual objects. Local operations are things like random point drop out, frustum drop out, additive noise added to the object, intra-object mixing, and swapping regions between different objects.

For the third challenge, and also the second one, other works propose to add ground-truth objects from other point clouds to the scene for training. This kind of augmentation does mitigate the imbalance. But it does not take the network architecture into account. Reuse et al. show with a series of experiments that both local and global data augmentation for 3D object detection depend strongly on the dataset and also on the network architecture. So augmentations that depend on the network are beneficial.

We present a new data modification approach that is network-dependent and addresses the second and third challenges. (The first challenge we address indirectly, like prior work.) The main idea is to learn a subset of the elements of the scene which are meaningful for object detection. In line with the observation of Reuse et al., we define meaningfulness in the context of the network and not only of the scene. If we only consider this subset as the input, we can decrease the number of elements in the scene and we can also increase the class balance inside a given scene.

To realize this idea we focus on SoTA detection networks that transform the point cloud into voxels as the first step of their pipeline. The main reason to transfer the input to voxels is to reduce the size of the input, since only occupied voxels are processed after that. This is what lets these systems work on extremely large scenes. Another obvious benefit of voxels is that they impose structure on the input.

In this voxel-based setup, the meaningful voxels are, generally speaking, the ones where the model "struggles" to locate the objects. So the gradients have a major role in determining which voxels are meaningful. That is why we call our approach Gradient-based Voxel Selection (GraVoS).

We show that if we focus only on the meaningful voxels and remove the non-informative ones, most of the voxels we discard belong to the scene background. A few of the removed voxels belong to the prevalent classes, and almost none belong to the non-prevalent classes. This is different from dropout augmentation techniques, which reduce the number of elements randomly.

The figure shows our distribution balancing. Given a point cloud (cyan), the subset of meaningful voxels we select (salmon) contains a lot fewer points from the background (here the points are voxel centers), more points on objects of the Car class (the most prevalent class), and almost all of the points on objects of the Pedestrian and Cyclist classes.

Our method is general and can be applied to different voxel-based networks. Also it does not add any inference time cost. We show results on four SoTA networks, SECOND, Part-A^{2}, Voxel R-CNN and CenterPoint, on the well-established KITTI dataset. All the networks improve their performance, especially for the difficult categories Pedestrian and Cyclist. For example, on the moderate subset of the benchmark the performance of Part-A^{2} improves by 2.32\% & 1.15\% for the non-prevalent classes (Cyclist and Pedestrian), which is an error reduction of 8.20\% & 2.77\%, respectively.

So the main contributions of this paper are:

- A new & generic method for selecting "meaningful" voxels, called Gradient-based Voxel Selection.

- A training procedure that uses the selected voxels to improve 3D detection without additional data. The procedure combines information from different stages of the training of the model.

- Showing improved performance of four voxel-based SoTA detection methods, which cope both with the inherent class imbalance and with the foreground-background imbalance.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
3D object detection has gained increasing importance in both industry and academia due to its wide range of applications, including autonomous driving and robotics [1,2]. LiDAR sensors are the de-facto standard acquisition devices for capturing 3D outdoor scenes (see figure). They produce sparse and irregular 3D point clouds, which are used in a variety of scene perception and understanding tasks.

There are three prominent challenges in outdoor point cloud datasets for detection. The first is the small size of the datasets, in terms of the number of scenes. The second is the large number of points in the scene compared to the small number of points on the training examples (objects): a single scene might contain hundreds of thousands, or even millions, of points but only a handful of objects. The third is class imbalance, where some classes contain significantly more instances than others, which often results in lower predictive accuracy for the infrequent classes [3,4].

To handle the first challenge, it was proposed to enrich the dataset during training with global operations, applied to the whole point cloud, such as rotation along the Z-axis, random flips along the X-axis, and coordinate scaling [5,6,7]. We note that most methods that solve the second and third challenges indirectly solve the first one as well.

To solve the second challenge, it is suggested to augment the scene by local operations, applied to the points belonging to individual objects [8,9]. These include random point drop out, frustum drop out, additive noise added to the object, intra-object mixing, and swapping regions between different objects.

To solve the third challenge, as well as the second one, [10,11,12,5] propose to add ground-truth objects from different point clouds to the scene during training. This type of augmentation indeed mitigates the imbalance. However, it does not take the network architecture into account, even though Reuse et al. [13] show, through a series of experiments, that both local and global data augmentation for 3D object detection strongly depend not only on the dataset but also on the network architecture. Network-dependent augmentations are therefore beneficial.

We present a novel network-dependent data modification approach that addresses the latter two challenges. (We address the first challenge indirectly, similarly to [10,11,12].) The key idea is to learn a subset of the elements of the scene that are meaningful for object detection. In line with [13]'s observation, meaningfulness is defined in the context of the network and not only of the scene. Considering only this subset as input allows us not only to decrease the number of elements in the scene but also to increase the class balance within a given scene.

To realize this idea, we focus on SoTA detection networks that transform point clouds into voxels as the first step of their pipeline. The main reason for transferring the input to voxels is to reduce the size of the input, as only the occupied voxels are then processed, which enables these systems to work on extremely large scenes. Another obvious benefit of voxels is the ability to impose structure on the input.

Generally speaking, in this voxel-based setup, meaningful voxels are those for which the model "struggles" to locate the objects. Hence, the gradients play a major role in determining the meaningful voxels, and our approach is termed Gradient-based Voxel Selection (GraVoS).

We show that when focusing only on the meaningful voxels and removing the non-informative ones, most of the discarded voxels belong to the scene background. Few of the removed voxels are associated with the prevalent classes, and almost none with the non-prevalent classes. Our strategy may be contrasted with dropout augmentation techniques, which reduce the number of elements randomly [8,9].

Our distribution balancing is demonstrated in the figure. Given a point cloud (cyan), our selected subset of meaningful voxels (salmon) contains significantly fewer points from the background (the points here are voxel centers), more points on objects belonging to the Car class (the most prevalent class), and almost all the points on objects belonging to the Pedestrian and Cyclist classes.

Our method is general and may be applied to different voxel-based networks, and it comes at no additional inference time cost. We show results on four SoTA networks: SECOND [5], Part-A^{2} [12], Voxel R-CNN [14], and CenterPoint [15] on the well-established KITTI dataset [16,1]. The performance of all networks improves, in particular for the difficult categories of Pedestrian and Cyclist. For instance, the performance of [12] on the benchmark's moderate subset improves by 2.32\% & 1.15\% for the non-prevalent classes (Cyclist and Pedestrian), an error reduction of 8.20\% & 2.77\%, respectively.

The main contributions of this paper are thus:

- A novel & generic "meaningful" voxel selection method, called Gradient-based Voxel Selection.

- A training procedure that uses the selected voxels to improve 3D detection without additional data, combining information from different stages of the model's training.

- Demonstrating improved performance of four voxel-based SoTA detection methods, which successfully cope both with the inherent class imbalance and with the foreground-background imbalance.

References:

[2] Sebastian Thrun, Mike Montemerlo, Hendrik Dahlkamp, David Stavens, Andrei Aron, James Diebel, Philip Fong, John Gale, Morgan Halpenny, Gabriel Hoffmann, et al. Stanley: The robot that won the darpa grand challenge. Journal of field Robotics , 23(9):661–692, 2006.
